questions.question: What does crontab stand for in Linux?

explanation.correct: Crontab stands for Cron Table — a file that lists scheduled tasks for the cron daemon.
explanation.why: B and C are not standard names. D is descriptively close but the official term is 'Cron Table'.

questions.question: What is the correct field order in a crontab expression?

options.text: Hour, Minute, Day of Month, Month, Day of Week
Minute, Hour, Day of Month, Month, Day of Week
Minute, Hour, Month, Day of Month, Day of Week

explanation.correct: The correct order is: Minute (0–59), Hour (0–23), Day of Month (1–31), Month (1–12), Day of Week (0–7).
explanation.why: This is a frequently tested fact — the minute field always comes first, not the hour.

questions.question: What does an asterisk (*) mean in a crontab field?

options.text: Every possible value for that field

explanation.correct: An asterisk (*) in any crontab field means 'every' — every minute, every hour, every day, depending on position.
explanation.why: A and B are incorrect. D is wrong — # is used for comments in crontab.

questions.question: Which command opens the crontab file for editing?

explanation.correct: crontab -e opens the crontab file in the default editor for the current user.
explanation.why: crontab -l lists jobs, crontab -r removes ALL jobs (dangerous), crontab -u specifies a user.

questions.question: What does crontab -r do?

options.text: Removes the current user's entire crontab — permanently

explanation.correct: crontab -r immediately deletes ALL scheduled jobs for the current user with no confirmation prompt.
explanation.why: This is a dangerous command — there is no undo. Always double-check before running it.

questions.question: What is an inode in Linux?

options.text: A data structure storing file metadata and data location but not the file name

explanation.correct: An inode stores metadata (permissions, owner, size, disk location) about a file — but NOT the file's name. The name is stored in the directory entry.
explanation.why: File names are stored separately from inodes — this distinction is the foundation of how hard links work.

questions.question: What is a hard link?

options.text: A shortcut that stores the path to another file
An additional directory entry pointing to the same inode as the original file
A copy of a file with a new inode

explanation.correct: A hard link creates another name that points to the same inode — the same actual data on disk. Both names are equal; neither is 'more original' than the other.
explanation.why: A describes a soft link. C describes a file copy. D is not a real concept.

questions.question: What is a soft link (symbolic link)?

options.text: A file that shares the same inode as another file
A file that contains the path to another file

explanation.correct: A soft link (symlink) is a special file whose content is simply the path to the target file — like a Windows desktop shortcut.
explanation.why: A describes a hard link. C and D describe unrelated concepts.

questions.question: What does wget stand for?

explanation.correct: wget stands for Web GET — it is a non-interactive command-line file downloader for retrieving files from the internet.
explanation.why: Only 'Web GET' is the correct expansion of wget.

questions.question: What does curl stand for?

explanation.correct: curl stands for Client URL — it is a data transfer tool supporting HTTP, HTTPS, FTP, and many other protocols.
explanation.why: Only 'Client URL' is the official expansion.

questions.question: Which crontab expression runs a job every day at 2:00 AM?

explanation.correct: 0 2 * * * means: minute=0, hour=2, every day, every month, every weekday — which is 2:00 AM daily.
explanation.why: A is 0:02 AM. C is every minute during hour 2. D is every hour on the 2nd day of the month.

questions.question: What happens to a soft link when the original file it points to is deleted?

options.text: The soft link automatically updates to point to the nearest file
The soft link becomes a regular file containing the path string
The soft link breaks — accessing it gives 'No such file or directory'
The soft link is also automatically deleted

explanation.correct: When the original file is deleted, a soft link becomes a dangling (broken) link. Attempting to access it returns an error.
explanation.why: Soft links store only a path. If the path no longer resolves to a file, the link is broken — it does not auto-update or delete itself.

questions.question: What happens to a hard link when the original file is deleted?

options.text: The hard link also gets deleted
The hard link breaks like a soft link
The hard link continues to work because the data (inode) is still present
The hard link converts to a soft link automatically

explanation.correct: A hard link shares the same inode as the original. Deleting one name only removes that directory entry — the inode and data remain as long as at least one link points to it.
explanation.why: This is a key exam distinction: hard links survive original deletion; soft links break.

questions.question: Which command lists files with their inode numbers?

explanation.correct: ls -li shows the inode number as the first column for each file. Two files with the same inode number are hard links to the same data.
explanation.why: ls -l shows permissions and size but not inode. ls -a shows hidden files. ls -n shows numeric UIDs instead of names.

questions.question: What does */6 mean in the hour field of a crontab expression?

options.text: 6 times per day at random times

explanation.correct: */6 in the hour field is a step value meaning 'every 6 hours' — it triggers at midnight, 6 AM, noon, and 6 PM.
explanation.why: Step values (*/n) divide the range into equal intervals. */6 in hours = every 6 hours from 0.

questions.question: What is the key difference between curl and wget?

options.text: wget supports HTTPS; curl does not
curl can send POST requests and set headers; wget is primarily for downloading files
curl is only for downloading; wget handles API calls
They are identical tools with different names

explanation.correct: curl is a versatile data transfer tool supporting full HTTP methods (GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), custom headers, and request bodies. wget is focused on non-interactive file downloading.
explanation.why: Both support HTTPS. They have different strengths — curl for API interaction, wget for reliable file downloads.

questions.question: Which flag tells curl to save a downloaded file using its original filename from the URL?

explanation.correct: curl -O (capital O) saves the file using the name from the URL. curl -o (lowercase) lets you specify a custom output filename.
explanation.why: This is a common exam gotcha — capital O uses original name, lowercase o takes a custom name argument.

questions.question: Which crontab expression runs a job every Sunday at 1:00 AM?

explanation.correct: 0 1 * * 0 means: minute=0, hour=1, every day-of-month, every month, Sunday (day 0 or 7). This runs every Sunday at 1:00 AM.
explanation.why: Day 0 and Day 7 both represent Sunday in crontab. Day 1 is Monday. * in minute means every minute of the hour.

questions.question: Can a hard link point to a file on a different file system or partition?

options.text: Yes — hard links work across all partitions
No — hard links can only exist within the same file system
Only if both file systems are ext4

explanation.correct: Hard links share an inode, and inodes only exist within a single file system. Cross-partition links are not possible with hard links — use soft links instead.
explanation.why: Soft links can cross file systems because they store a path (not an inode reference). Hard links are limited to the same partition.

questions.question: Which curl flag sends a POST request?

explanation.correct: curl -X POST specifies the HTTP method as POST. -X followed by the method name works for GET, POST, PUT, DELETE, etc.
explanation.why: Only -X is the correct flag for specifying request method in curl.

questions.question: How does AWS EventBridge use cron expressions?

options.text: Only to set instance launch times
To schedule automated AWS actions like triggering Lambda functions at specified times

explanation.correct: Amazon EventBridge uses cron expressions (and rate expressions) to schedule automated AWS actions — such as triggering Lambda functions, stopping EC2 instances, or invoking Step Functions on a schedule.
explanation.why: This is a key AWS integration: Linux crontab knowledge directly maps to EventBridge scheduled rules.

questions.question: What URL do you use to query EC2 instance metadata from inside an EC2 instance?

explanation.correct: The EC2 metadata service is available at the link-local address http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ — only accessible from inside the EC2 instance itself.
explanation.why: This is a heavily tested AWS fact. The IP 169.254.169.254 is a link-local address — not routable from outside the instance.

questions.question: You want to download a large file and need the ability to resume if the connection drops. Which tool is better?

options.text: Both tools have identical resume capabilities

explanation.correct: wget -c (or --continue) enables resumable downloads — it can pick up where it left off if interrupted. This is one of wget's key advantages for large file downloads.
explanation.why: While curl can also resume with -C -, wget's -c flag is simpler and designed for exactly this use case.

questions.question: A crontab expression is: 30 9-17 * * 1-5. What does this mean?

options.text: Run at minute 30 of every hour between 9 AM and 5 PM, Monday to Friday
Run at 9:30 AM and 5:30 PM on weekdays

explanation.correct: 30 = minute 30, 9-17 = hours 9 through 17 (9 AM to 5 PM), * * = every day of month, every month, 1-5 = Monday to Friday. So it runs at :30 past each hour from 9:30 AM to 5:30 PM on weekdays.
explanation.why: Ranges (9-17) select all values in that range. This combines hour ranges with weekday ranges for business-hours scheduling.

questions.question: Two files have different inode numbers but the same content. What were they created with?

options.text: A hard link with the -n flag

explanation.correct: A hard link shares the same inode (same inode number). A soft link has its own inode but stores a path. If two files have different inodes but the same content, they are independent copies created with cp.
explanation.why: The key distinguisher: same inode = hard link. Different inode but identical content = copy.

questions.question: What does the cron expression 0 0 1 * * mean?

options.text: Midnight on the 1st of every month

explanation.correct: 0 0 1 * * means: minute=0, hour=0 (midnight), day-of-month=1, every month, every weekday — so midnight on the 1st of each month.
explanation.why: The third field is day-of-month. Setting it to 1 means only the 1st day of each month.

questions.question: Which ln command flag creates a soft link instead of a hard link?

explanation.correct: ln -s creates a symbolic (soft) link. Without -s, ln creates a hard link by default.
explanation.why: The -s flag is critical to know — it's the only difference between hard and soft link creation commands.

questions.question: A soft link in ls -l output starts with which letter?

explanation.correct: In ls -l output, the first character indicates file type: l = symbolic link, d = directory, - = regular file, b = block device.
explanation.why: This is a practical identification skill. A broken soft link still shows as 'l' but is typically displayed in red.

questions.question: You want to use curl to send a JSON payload to a REST API endpoint. Which flags are required?

explanation.correct: To send JSON with curl you need: -X POST (method), -H 'Content-Type: application/json' (tell server it's JSON), and -d '{...}' (the JSON body data).
explanation.why: Without the Content-Type header, the server may not correctly parse the JSON body. All three flags work together.

questions.question: What is the purpose of export EDITOR=nano before running crontab -e?

options.text: It installs the nano editor on the system
It creates an environment variable telling all programs in this terminal to use nano as the default editor
It permanently changes the default editor for all future terminal sessions
It only affects the crontab command, not other programs

explanation.correct: export creates an environment variable and makes it available to all child processes spawned from the current terminal. Setting EDITOR=nano tells every program that needs to open an editor — including crontab -e — to use nano.
explanation.why: export makes the variable available to child processes. Without export, the variable would only be available in the current shell, not in programs it launches. It only lasts for the current session.

questions.question: Which crontab expression restarts a service every 6 hours?

explanation.correct: 0 */6 * * * means: minute=0, hour=every 6th hour (*/6), every day, every month, every weekday — triggers at 0:00, 6:00, 12:00, 18:00.
explanation.why: */6 in the hour field means 'every 6 hours starting from 0'. The 0 in the minute field ensures it runs at exactly :00 of those hours, not every minute during those hours.

questions.question: Can a hard link be created for a directory?

options.text: Yes — same as for regular files
No — hard links to directories are generally not allowed (except by root for special purposes)

explanation.correct: Hard links to directories are prohibited in most Linux systems to prevent circular directory structures and filesystem corruption. Soft links to directories are allowed and commonly used.
explanation.why: This is a key hard link limitation — if you need a link to a directory, always use a soft link (ln -s).
